items.d: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic; Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty, Equality, Fraternity — dignity of the individual and unity and **integrity** of the nation. 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'integrity' were inserted by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**. Held to be **part of the Constitution and amendable but not its basic structure** in *Kesavananda* and reaffirmed in 2024.

India, that is Bharat, shall be a **Union of States** — Ambedkar: the Union is not the result of an agreement among states and no state has the **right to secede**. The textual anchor for 'indestructible union of destructible states'.

Art. 2 admits or establishes **new** states; **Art. 3** forms new states and alters areas, boundaries or names of existing states — needs the **President's recommendation** and reference to the state legislature **whose view is not binding**. Basis of linguistic reorganisation and of Telangana (2014) and the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019.

Citizenship at commencement; **Art. 11** empowers Parliament to regulate citizenship by law — hence the **Citizenship Act, 1955** and its amendments (1986, 2003 introducing the NRC/NPR framework, and 2019). Citizenship is a **Union subject (List I, Entry 17)**.

Definition of **'State'** — includes Government and Parliament of India, state governments and legislatures, **local authorities and 'other authorities'**. 'Other authorities' extended to instrumentalities of the state by the six-fold test in *Ajay Hasia* and *R.D. Shetty*; BCCI held amenable to writ jurisdiction for public functions.

Laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are **void** — the textual basis of **judicial review**. Carries the doctrines of **severability**, **eclipse**, and **waiver is not permitted** (a citizen cannot waive a fundamental right — *Basheshar Nath*). **Art. 13(4)** excludes constitutional amendments, which is why *Kesavananda* had to build basic structure.

Equality before law (Dicey's negative concept) and equal protection of the laws (positive). Tests: **reasonable classification** (intelligible differentia + rational nexus) and, since *E.P. Royappa*, the **arbitrariness test** — 'equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies'. Extended to **manifest arbitrariness** of legislation in *Shayara Bano*.

15(1) bars discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth; **15(3)** special provisions for women and children; **15(4)** SEBC/SC/ST advancement; **15(5)** private unaided institutions (93rd Amendment); **15(6)** and **16(6)** EWS 10% (103rd Amendment, upheld in *Janhit Abhiyan* 2022). 16(4) reservation in appointments; **16(4A)** promotion with consequential seniority; **16(4B)** carry-forward of backlog vacancies.

**Abolition of untouchability** — the only fundamental right enforceable against private individuals as well; operationalised through the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the **SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989**. Invoked in *Sabarimala* by Chandrachud J. to cover exclusion based on notions of purity and pollution.

**19(1)(a)-(g)** six freedoms, each with its own reasonableness clause (19(2)-(6)); **Art. 21** life and personal liberty, transformed by *Maneka Gandhi* into a **'procedure established by law' that must be just, fair and reasonable** — importing substantive due process. The **golden triangle is Articles 14, 19 and 21** (*Minerva Mills*).

Read into Art. 21: **privacy** (*Puttaswamy* 2017), **clean environment** (*Subhash Kumar*), **livelihood** (*Olga Tellis*), **speedy trial** (*Hussainara Khatoon*), **legal aid** (*M.H. Hoskot*), **shelter**, **health**, **dignity**, **against a clean environment free of climate impacts** (*M.K. Ranjitsinh* 2024), **passive euthanasia and living wills** (*Common Cause* 2018), and the **right to be forgotten** in emerging jurisprudence. Naming three with case-tags is worth more than listing ten.

**86th Amendment, 2002** made free and compulsory education for **6-14 years** a fundamental right (Art. 21A), moved the earlier Art. 45 directive to **early childhood care and education below 6**, and added the parental duty under **Art. 51A(k)**. Implemented by the **RTE Act, 2009**, upheld in *Society for Unaided Private Schools* (2012).

Protection against arrest and detention — right to be informed of grounds, to consult counsel, and production before a magistrate within **24 hours**; **but 22(3)** excludes enemy aliens and **preventive detention**. 22(4)-(7) permit detention up to **3 months** without an Advisory Board. India is the only major democracy with **peacetime preventive detention in the Constitution itself**.

**23** prohibits traffic in human beings and **begar/forced labour** — the basis of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 and of *PUDR v. Union of India* (1982), which held that **payment below minimum wage is forced labour**. **24** bars employment of children under 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work.

**25** freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion, subject to public order, morality, health and **the state's power to make social welfare and reform laws**; **26** rights of religious denominations; **27** no compulsion to pay taxes for promotion of a religion; **28** religious instruction in state-funded institutions. The **essential religious practices doctrine** comes from *Shirur Mutt* (1954).

**29** protects the language, script and culture of any section of citizens; **30** gives **minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions**, and 30(1A) requires that compensation on acquisition not defeat that right. *T.M.A. Pai* (2002) fixed the **state as the unit** for determining minority status; *Aligarh Muslim University* (2024) overruled *Azeez Basha* and laid down the **indicia test** for minority character.

Right to constitutional remedies — Ambedkar's **"heart and soul of the Constitution"**. Five writs: **habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto**. Art. 32 is itself a fundamental right and **cannot be suspended except under Art. 359** during an emergency; the SC's power under 32 is part of the **basic structure**.

The **44th Amendment, 1978** deleted the right to property from Part III and made it a **constitutional right under Article 300A** ('no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law'). *Minerva Mills* struck down the extension of Art. 31C protection to all DPSPs, restoring the balance between Parts III and IV.

**39(b)-(c)** material resources and concentration of wealth; **39A** equal justice and free legal aid (42nd Amendment); **40** organisation of village panchayats; **41** right to work, education and public assistance; **43** living wage; **43B** cooperative societies (97th Amendment); **44** uniform civil code; **47** nutrition and public health, prohibition of intoxicants; **48A** environment, forests and wildlife (42nd); **50** separation of judiciary from executive.

**Eleven Fundamental Duties**, inserted by the **42nd Amendment, 1976** on the **Swaran Singh Committee's** recommendation, with 51A(k) added by the 86th. Non-justiciable, but the **Verma Committee (1999)** listed existing statutes that operationalise them, and courts use them as an interpretive aid.

**53** executive power vested in the President; **74** Council of Ministers **aid and advise**, binding after the **42nd Amendment**, with a **one-time return for reconsideration** added by the 44th; **75(3)** collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha; **76** Attorney General; **78** the PM's duty to communicate Council decisions to the President — the constitutional basis of the President's right to be informed.

**Pardoning power** — President (72) covers court martial, offences against Union law, and **all death sentences**; Governor (161) is narrower. It is an **executive act, exercised on ministerial advice**, and is **judicially reviewable on limited grounds** — non-application of mind, mala fides, or irrelevant considerations. Undue delay in deciding a mercy petition is a ground to commute.
items.s: Maru Ram (1980) / Epuru Sudhakar (2006) / Shatrughan Chauhan (2014)

items.d: **Ordinance-making power** of the President and Governor, exercisable only when the legislature is not in session and immediate action is necessary. *Krishna Kumar Singh* (2017) held that **re-promulgation is a fraud on the Constitution** and that ordinances must be laid before the legislature — satisfaction is subject to judicial review. Bihar's 256 re-promulgated ordinances over 1967-81 is the standing example.

**155** appointed by the President; **156** holds office **during the President's pleasure** — no fixed tenure; **163** aids-and-advises except where he acts in his discretion, and **the question of what falls in discretion is non-justiciable in form but reviewable in substance**; **164(1)** appoints the CM; **200** assent to bills; **361** immunity. The Sarkaria, Punchhi and Venkatachaliah reports all recommended appointment from a panel proposed by the state and removal only for proven misconduct.

The Governor may assent, withhold assent, return a non-money bill for reconsideration, or **reserve it for the President**. The **first proviso requires a return 'as soon as possible'**; if the House passes it again, the Governor **shall not withhold assent**. The Supreme Court has read **timelines into what the text leaves open** and held that indefinite inaction — the 'pocket veto' — is unconstitutional. The Presidential Reference of 2025 arose from this line of cases.
items.s: State of Punjab v. Governor (2023) / State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor (2025)

items.d: President's Rule on failure of constitutional machinery. *S.R. Bommai* (1994) made the proclamation **justiciable**, held that the **floor of the House is the only test of majority**, that the Assembly may be dissolved only **after both Houses of Parliament approve**, and that **secularism is a basic feature** — a state government acting against secularism can be dismissed. Recommended for use only in extreme cases by the **Sarkaria Commission**.

**79** Parliament = President + two Houses; **80** Rajya Sabha up to 250 (238 elected by **single transferable vote** by state assemblies + 12 nominated); **81** Lok Sabha up to 550; **83** terms — LS five years, RS a permanent body with **one-third retiring every two years**; **88** ministers and the AG have the right to speak in either House.

**100** quorum is **one-tenth** of the total membership; **108** **joint sitting** to resolve a deadlock on an ordinary or financial (not money) bill — used only **three times**: Dowry Prohibition Act (1961), Banking Service Commission Repeal (1978) and the **POTA (2002)**. The Speaker presides over a joint sitting.

**109** money bills originate only in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha has **14 days and only recommendatory power**; **110** defines a money bill and the **Speaker's certification is final**; **112** Annual Financial Statement; **113-114** demands for grants and the Appropriation Bill; **266** Consolidated Fund; **267** Contingency Fund; **117** prior recommendation of the President for financial bills. The money-bill route used for Aadhaar was upheld in *Puttaswamy (Aadhaar)* but doubted in *Rojer Mathew* and referred to a larger bench.

Freedom of speech in Parliament and immunity from proceedings for anything said or any vote given. **Sita Soren (2024)**, a **seven-judge bench, overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998)**, holding that a legislator who takes a **bribe for a vote or speech enjoys no immunity** — the offence is complete on acceptance and is not 'essential to' the legislative function. Privileges remain **uncodified**, the standing reform demand.
items.s: Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024)

items.d: Inserted by the **52nd Amendment, 1985**; the **91st Amendment, 2003** deleted the split (one-third) exception and required a **merger of two-thirds**. *Kihoto Hollohan* (1992) upheld it but made the **Speaker's decision subject to judicial review**; *Keisham Meghachandra* (2020) said the Speaker should decide **within three months** and suggested an independent tribunal; *Subhash Desai* (2023) held that a **Whip is appointed by the party, not the legislature party**.

**PAC (1921, 22 members, chaired by the Opposition by convention)**, **Estimates Committee (1950, 30 members, LS only — 'continuous economy committee')**, **COPU (1964, 22)**; **24 Department-Related Standing Committees since 1993** (16 LS + 8 RS, 31 members each), which examine demands for grants, bills and long-term policy. Ministers are not members of DRSCs. Committee scrutiny of bills has fallen sharply — the standing critique of parliamentary decline.
items.s: Rules of Procedure / PRS Legislative Research

items.d: **124** establishment and appointment; **124A-C** were the NJAC provisions struck down in 2015; **126** acting CJI; **127-128** ad hoc and retired judges; **129** court of record with contempt power; **131** original jurisdiction in Centre-state disputes; **136** **Special Leave Petition**, the discretionary residual power; **137** review; **141** law declared is binding on all courts; **142** **complete justice**; **143** advisory jurisdiction, which the Court may decline.

Power to pass any decree necessary for **complete justice**. Used for the **Ayodhya** settlement, the **Babri** structure, the **2G** cancellation, dissolving marriages on **irretrievable breakdown** (*Shilpa Sailesh*, 2023), and in *State of Punjab v. Governor* to fix timelines. Also the subject of the sharpest separation-of-powers criticism — powers under 142 cannot **supplant substantive law**.

High Courts; **Art. 226 is wider than Art. 32** — it issues writs for fundamental rights **and for 'any other purpose'**, and its territorial reach extends to where the cause of action arises. *L. Chandra Kumar* (1997) held that the **High Courts' power of judicial review under 226/227 is part of the basic structure** and tribunals cannot oust it.

**246** and the **Seventh Schedule**: Union List 97, State List 59 (originally 66), Concurrent List 52 (originally 47). **248** residuary power with the Union; **249** RS resolution by two-thirds enabling Parliament to legislate on a State List item in the national interest; **250** during emergency; **252** two or more states requesting; **253** to implement international agreements; **254** **repugnancy**, with state law prevailing if it receives **Presidential assent**. Doctrines: **pith and substance, colourable legislation, harmonious construction**.

**262** inter-state **river water disputes** — Parliament may bar the jurisdiction of all courts, done by the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956; **263** empowers the President to establish an **Inter-State Council** — done in 1990 on the **Sarkaria Commission's** recommendation. The ISC is an advisory, recommendatory body that has met rarely; the **Punchhi Commission** wanted it strengthened into the primary forum for federal consultation.

Created by the **101st Amendment, 2016**. Voting: **Centre one-third, all states together two-thirds, decisions by a three-fourths majority**; quorum one-half. *Mohit Minerals* (2022) held that **the Council's recommendations are persuasive, not binding**, because both Parliament and state legislatures have simultaneous power under Art. 246A — described by the Court as **'cooperative federalism as dialogue'**.
items.s: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022)

items.d: **280** Finance Commission every five years — devolution, grants-in-aid under Art. 275, and measures to augment state funds for local bodies. **148-151** the **CAG** — appointed by the President, removable like a SC judge, salary charged on the Consolidated Fund, **barred from further office** under the Union or a state after retirement; reports go to the President/Governor and are examined by the PAC.

UPSC and State PSCs; **316** appointment by the President/Governor, **at least half the members must have held office under the Government for ten years**; **317** removal **only by the President on a Supreme Court reference**; **319** post-retirement bar (a UPSC chairman is ineligible for any further government employment); **320** functions; **322** expenses charged on the Consolidated Fund; **323** annual report laid before the legislature with a memorandum on non-acceptance of advice.

**Tribunals** (42nd Amendment) — administrative tribunals (323A, Parliament only) and other-matter tribunals (323B). **324** vests superintendence, direction and control of elections in the **Election Commission**; the CEC and ECs are now appointed under the **CEC and Other ECs Act, 2023**, enacted after *Anoop Baranwal* (2023) had prescribed a CJI-inclusive panel. The CEC can be removed only like a SC judge; other ECs only on the CEC's recommendation.

**NCSC (338)**, **NCST (338A, created by the 89th Amendment, 2003)** and **NCBC (338B, given constitutional status by the 102nd Amendment, 2018)** — all have the powers of a civil court and must be consulted on major policy affecting their groups. **350B** Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities. The **105th Amendment, 2021** restored the states' power to identify their own SEBCs after *Maratha Reservation* (2021).

**73rd and 74th Amendments, 1992** — three tiers above 20 lakh population, five-year terms, **State Election Commission (243K/243ZA)**, **State Finance Commission every five years (243I/243Y)**, **one-third seats for women** (many states now 50%), **Eleventh Schedule 29 subjects** and **Twelfth Schedule 18 subjects**, **District Planning Committee (243ZD)** and **Metropolitan Planning Committee (243ZE)**. Devolution of functions, funds and functionaries remains discretionary — the core weakness.

**Fifth Schedule** — Scheduled Areas in ten states, Governor's report to the President, **Tribes Advisory Council**, and the Governor's power to modify central or state laws for the area. **Sixth Schedule** — **Autonomous District Councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram** with legislative, judicial and financial powers over land, forests and customary law. **PESA, 1996** extends Part IX to Scheduled Areas with the gram sabha as the competent authority.
